(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) — Sound the alarm and keep your family close: DreamWorks Animation has unleashed yet another oversized, extravagantly manufactured, premise-driven creation aimed at young audiences. In “Monsters vs. Aliens,” Susan—renamed “Ginormica”—must rescue the planet.

Still, there is little reason to panic. The film is mostly innocuous: a feeble satire built around an automatic feminist message and barely supported by a plot. That judgment may seem severe. After all, who could resist watching a 50-foot woman hurtle through San Francisco on roller skates made from cars, creating the ultimate destructive roller derby?

Pause to consider the mechanics, though. Roller skates function because their wheels remain fixed in place; automobiles would not carry you very far in the same fashion. Is that an overly fussy objection? Maybe. Yet Pixar would be unlikely to disregard basic physics so casually. That carelessness reflects the generally sloppy storytelling found here and in other animated DreamWorks productions. For the record, the creative team includes directors associated with “Shrek 2” and “Shark Tale,” along with writers whose credits include “Kung Fu Panda” and “The Rocker.”

A big premise, celebrated voice actors and randomly deployed pop-culture allusions cannot replace a logically constructed screenplay.

The enormous heroine whom her U.S. military captors name Ginormica begins as Susan Murphy, an ordinary, small-statured woman voiced by Reese Witherspoon. Moments before she is due to marry the oily, sexist Derek, played by Paul Rudd, Susan is struck by a meteorite. Her sudden transformation into a giant at least spares her from that fate worse than death, although her new companions initially appear no more appealing.

They include Dr. Cockroach, voiced by Hugh Laurie, an unhinged scientist who more or less accidentally combined himself with an insect; B.O.B., played by Seth Rogen, a shapeless blue gelatinous mass who manages perfectly well despite lacking a brain; and Missing Link, voiced by Will Arnett, an aggressive amphibious creature distinguished mainly by his mouth. There is also Insectosaurus, an immense dust mite with no voice actor because the character has nothing to say.

Science-fiction enthusiasts can amuse themselves by identifying nods to numerous genre landmarks. Among the obvious sources are “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” “Invaders from Mars,” “The Fly,” “The Creature from the Black Lagoon,” “The Blob,” “Mothra” and “Attack of the 50-Foot Woman.” A handful of details are genuinely inventive, including Kiefer Sutherland’s performance as General W.R. Monger, which echoes George C. Scott in “Dr. Strangelove.”

Unfortunately, after presenting its characters, the movie has nowhere to go except into an embarrassingly weak storyline. The White House recruits these monstrous heroes to defend Earth against Gallaxhar, voiced by Rainn Wilson. The villain is a squidlike being with four eyes and eight legs who relies on a one-eyed metal robot to carry out his plans.

Ginormica is rewarded with an action-heavy conclusion, and she emerges as a far more powerful figure—in several senses—than the movie’s president. In one truly inspired piece of casting, that president is voiced by Stephen Colbert.

From the studio’s standpoint, making Susan so formidable may represent either admirable politics or smart marketing. Family animation had not produced a convincingly strong female protagonist for some time, unless “Coraline” qualifies—and that film was much too frightening for my family. Even so, Susan takes far too long to develop confidence in herself.

iReport.com: Share your opinion of “Monsters vs. Aliens.”

Strangely—and perhaps this is only in the eye of the reviewer—Gallaxhar looks somewhat like President Obama. If so, does that position Susan/Ginormica as a stand-in for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?

The film is no more remarkable visually than it is narratively, though seeing it in 3-D may conceal some of those weaknesses. It is curious how often three-dimensional filmmaking results in flat characters; once again, “Coraline” is the notable exception.

With its playful tone and cheerfully lowbrow sensibility, “Monsters vs. Aliens” ought to be thoroughly enjoyable, and occasionally it is. Ultimately, however, the movie is every bit as self-satisfied as Susan’s vain fiancé. Honestly, “Space Chimps” provided a more entertaining experience.

“Monsters vs. Aliens” has a running time of 94 minutes and carries a PG rating. Follow the link for Entertainment Weekly’s review.

DreamWorks’ *Monsters vs. Aliens* begins with a promisingly absurd idea: on her wedding day, an ordinary young woman named Susan Murphy is struck by a meteorite and grows to nearly fifty feet tall. The government promptly captures her, renames her Ginormica, and confines her in a secret facility with a collection of monsters left over from old science-fiction movies. When an alien invader arrives to reclaim the substance that caused Susan’s transformation, the imprisoned creatures are recruited to save the world.

The giant-woman premise gives the film its strongest material. Susan’s sudden change literalizes her struggle to outgrow the small life planned for her, particularly her engagement to a self-absorbed television weatherman. At first she wants only to return to normal, but she gradually recognizes that her former fiancé valued her mainly as an accessory to his ambitions. Becoming enormous allows her to discover a confidence and independence she did not possess before. The feminist message is obvious but welcome: Susan does not need to shrink herself, physically or emotionally, to make an inadequate man comfortable.

Unfortunately, the screenplay rarely develops that idea beyond the most basic level. Susan’s transformation is less the foundation of a carefully constructed story than an excuse for chases, collisions, landmarks in peril, and 3-D objects thrust toward the audience. The film’s physics are similarly slapdash. Susan’s size, strength, weight, and vulnerability change according to the demands of each scene, while the alien technology and monster abilities operate without meaningful rules. Cartoon logic is not inherently a flaw, but successful animated films usually establish an internal consistency that makes even outrageous action feel convincing. Here, spectacle repeatedly substitutes for coherence.

The supporting monsters are introduced efficiently, if mechanically. There is Dr. Cockroach, a brilliant scientist with an insect’s head; the Missing Link, an aquatic ape-man; B.O.B., an indestructible blue blob with no brain; and Insectosaurus, a colossal grub treated largely as a visual gag. Each character is based on a familiar 1950s monster-movie archetype, and the group’s mismatched personalities provide the expected comic friction. Yet they seldom become more than collections of quirks. B.O.B. is cheerfully stupid, the Missing Link is vain and macho, and Dr. Cockroach speaks in a theatrical mad-scientist manner. Their friendship with Susan is pleasant but underwritten, developing because the plot requires a team rather than because the characters form especially persuasive bonds.

The celebrity voice cast adds energy without solving the problem. Reese Witherspoon gives Susan warmth and determination, Seth Rogen supplies B.O.B. with amiable foolishness, Hugh Laurie enjoys Dr. Cockroach’s exaggerated villainous cadence, and Will Arnett brings swagger to the Missing Link. Rainn Wilson voices the alien Gallaxhar, while Stephen Colbert plays the president as an incompetent caricature. The performers are recognizable and capable, but the movie often seems to rely on their personas instead of giving them memorable dialogue or emotional depth.

Much of the humor comes from pop-culture references and broad parody. The film gestures toward classic creature features, alien-invasion stories, political satire, science-fiction clichés, and more contemporary entertainment. Some jokes are amusing in isolation, especially the president’s attempt to communicate with the alien vessel through music. But the references accumulate without creating a distinctive comic point of view. Rather than using parody to illuminate the genres it borrows from, the movie frequently treats recognition itself as the punch line.

That tendency reflects a broader weakness in DreamWorks animation. The studio’s films can be bright, fast, and professionally assembled, yet they often advertise their cleverness too loudly. *Monsters vs. Aliens* is packed with activity, but little of it feels carefully observed. Plot developments occur because another action sequence is needed, emotional turns arrive on schedule, and potentially interesting ideas are abandoned as soon as they have served a joke. Pixar’s best films, by contrast, tend to build worlds in which visual details, character motivations, humor, and theme reinforce one another. The difference is not simply sentiment or technical polish; it is attention to narrative detail.

The movie is not unpleasant. Its violence is harmless, its message is broadly positive, and younger viewers may enjoy the colorful creatures and large-scale destruction. Susan is an appealing heroine, and the decision to let her embrace her transformed identity rather than retreat into conventional romance gives the ending some force. Even so, the satire remains toothless, the villain is thinly conceived, and the running time feels bloated by repetitive action.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* ultimately resembles one of its own giant set pieces: shiny, noisy, and momentarily diverting, but less substantial than it first appears. Its giant-woman premise and feminist undertones suggest a sharper, stranger film than the one DreamWorks actually made. What remains is a relatively harmless entertainment whose flashy spectacle and celebrity voices cannot compensate for a weak plot, inconsistent logic, and an overreliance on familiar jokes.

## Review: “Monsters vs. Aliens” is big, loud and disappointingly hollow

DreamWorks Animation’s “Monsters vs. Aliens” assembles an all-star voice cast, raids decades of science-fiction history and wraps a story of female empowerment in eye-popping 3-D. Yet beneath its polished surface is a frustratingly mechanical comedy—one that mistakes frantic references, celebrity voices and objects flying toward the audience for personality.

Reese Witherspoon voices Susan Murphy, a dutiful California bride whose wedding day is interrupted by a meteorite. The impact causes her to grow to 49 feet, 11 inches—apparently stopping one inch short of a more litigious title—and earns her the government codename Ginormica. She is promptly imprisoned alongside a collection of secret monsters: gelatinous dimwit B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), reptilian Missing Link (Will Arnett), mad scientist Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie) and skyscraper-sized Insectosaurus.

When the alien Gallaxhar, voiced with sneering relish by Rainn Wilson, invades Earth to retrieve the meteor’s powerful “quantonium,” the government releases the monsters under the command of Gen. W.R. Monger (Kiefer Sutherland). The misfits must save the planet that locked them away—a promising setup the film reduces to chases, explosions and predictable lessons about self-esteem.

The script is essentially a pop-culture recycling plant. Susan recalls “Attack of the 50 Foot Woman”; B.O.B. is a child-friendly Blob; Missing Link borrows from “Creature from the Black Lagoon”; Dr. Cockroach evokes “The Fly”; and Insectosaurus arrives by way of Japanese kaiju movies. There are nods to “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” “Dr. Strangelove” and generations of flying-saucer films. Some references will amuse adults, but too many function as substitutes for jokes rather than the foundation of them.

Stephen Colbert provides one of the livelier turns as an aggressively incompetent U.S. president, while Paul Rudd voices Susan’s vain, career-minded fiancé, Derek. The cast also includes Jeffrey Tambor, Renée Zellweger, Amy Poehler and John Krasinski. It is an impressive roster, though the movie often gives its performers little beyond a single comic setting: Rogen is clueless, Arnett is macho, Laurie is manic and Sutherland bellows military jargon.

The film’s most interesting element is Susan’s transformation. At first she wants only to become small again and return to Derek. Gradually, she recognizes that her new size is not a curse but a source of independence and strength. Her rejection of a selfish fiancé and embrace of her own power give the movie a plainly feminist arc.

But the message is blunted by the storytelling. Susan’s empowerment is expressed largely through physical size and combat ability, while the men around her are rendered so foolish, cowardly or narcissistic that her growth requires little emotional complexity. The film deserves credit for making a woman the unquestioned leader of an action team; it deserves less for treating that idea as revolutionary while surrounding her with cardboard caricatures.

Visually, “Monsters vs. Aliens” is slick and frequently spectacular. The scale of Ginormica and Insectosaurus is conveyed with playful camera angles, and the battle at the Golden Gate Bridge remains the movie’s strongest sequence. The 3-D effects, however, are often aggressively conspicuous: paddles, debris and various body parts lunge toward the viewer as if the filmmakers fear the audience might forget to appreciate the technology.

That anxiety defines the entire production. Every moment is busy, every character is shouting, and every emotional beat arrives prepackaged. The monsters are likable but thinly drawn, Gallaxhar is a generic villain, and the story moves too quickly to develop the outsider theme suggested by its premise.

“Monsters vs. Aliens” is not a disaster. It is colorful, energetic and harmless enough for younger viewers. But from a studio capable of sharper satire and richer characters, this is assembly-line animation inflated to giant size: impressive from a distance, noisy up close and, like B.O.B., missing something essential inside.

**Monsters vs. Aliens (2009) — Review**

DreamWorks’ *Monsters vs. Aliens* begins with an admirably efficient premise: take every 1950s creature-feature cliché, add celebrity voices, and fire the whole thing directly at the audience’s face in 3-D. Storytelling, apparently, was asked to stand a safe distance behind the screen.

Reese Witherspoon voices Susan, a bride struck by a meteor and transformed into the 49-foot-11-inch Ginormica. She’s promptly imprisoned alongside a genial blob named B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), the fish-ape Missing Link (Will Arnett), insect scientist Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), and the enormous Insectosaurus. When alien overlord Gallaxhar attacks Earth, the government releases the monsters to save humanity—a plan that makes perfect sense by the standards of both B-movies and federal bureaucracy.

The cast is lively, and B.O.B. gets most of the best gags, largely because a character without a brain is ideally positioned to navigate the screenplay. There are amusing references to old science-fiction films, some energetic action, and enough adult-friendly jokes to keep parents from checking the theater exits too often. But the plot is painfully familiar, the emotional beats arrive factory-sealed, and most characters are comic concepts rather than personalities.

This is where the Pixar comparison becomes unkind but unavoidable. Pixar’s best films use dazzling technology to support strong characters and emotionally precise storytelling. DreamWorks here seems to have reversed the process: it built the trailer moments first, then filled the gaps with noise, pop-culture riffs, and a lesson about self-acceptance that feels downloaded from a motivational screensaver.

The 3-D is impressive—objects swoop, missiles hurtle, and assorted limbs extend toward your popcorn with great enthusiasm. Yet the effects compensate for the weak storytelling only briefly. Depth on the screen cannot create depth in the script. Once the novelty fades, what remains is a bright, brisk, intermittently funny adventure that looks more substantial than it is.

**Verdict:** A visually polished, pleasantly silly diversion whose monsters are more memorable than its story. The 3-D gives it extra dimension; sadly, the characters could have used some too.

# A Giant Step for Her, a Familiar Leap for Animation  
**“Monsters vs. Aliens” offers lively 3-D spectacle, retro science-fiction wit and an unusually appealing heroine**

There is something wonderfully direct about the title **“Monsters vs. Aliens.”** No coy metaphors, no mystery and scarcely a noun wasted. DreamWorks Animation’s 2009 adventure promises colossal creatures, extraterrestrial invaders and enough airborne hardware to keep the screen in a near-permanent state of commotion. It delivers all three with considerable polish, even if its affection for old science-fiction movies is sometimes more memorable than its barrage of contemporary wisecracks.

The film’s smartest decision is to place a woman—not merely a princess, sidekick or romantic prize—at the center of the mayhem.

Susan Murphy, voiced with bright sincerity by **Reese Witherspoon**, begins the story on what is supposed to be the happiest day of her life. Moments before marrying Derek Dietl (**Paul Rudd**), a preening television weatherman with ambitions larger than his devotion, Susan is struck by a meteorite saturated with a rare substance called quantonium. During the ceremony she abruptly grows to a height of nearly 50 feet—49 feet, 11 inches, to preserve the film’s running joke—and is promptly captured by the military.

Renamed **Ginormica**, Susan is confined in a secret government facility with a collection of creatures that could have wandered out of a 1950s drive-in double feature. The prison is overseen by the swaggering, gravel-voiced **General W.R. Monger**, played by **Kiefer Sutherland**, who has spent decades keeping America’s monsters out of public view.

The inmates are an agreeably eccentric bunch. **Dr. Cockroach, Ph.D.** (**Hugh Laurie**) is a brilliant scientist whose attempt to give himself a cockroach’s indestructibility worked rather too well. **The Missing Link** (**Will Arnett**) is a boastful amphibious ape-man, discovered frozen and not nearly as formidable as he imagines. **B.O.B.** (**Seth Rogen**) is a cheerful blue gelatinous blob created when a genetically altered tomato was injected with ranch-flavored dessert topping. He has no brain, but he compensates with boundless enthusiasm and a talent for swallowing almost anything. Towering over them all is **Insectosaurus**, a 350-foot larva whose roars require no celebrity dialogue.

They receive their chance at freedom when the alien tyrant **Gallaxhar**—voiced by **Rainn Wilson** with theatrical petulance—arrives to retrieve the quantonium now coursing through Susan’s body. After conventional military weapons prove predictably useless, General Monger persuades the government to deploy the monsters. The resulting battles move from San Francisco’s Golden Gate Bridge to Gallaxhar’s immense spaceship, allowing the animators to alternate between broad comedy and gleaming destruction.

Directors **Rob Letterman and Conrad Vernon** treat science-fiction history as a vast toy chest. Susan’s transformation is the most obvious nod to *Attack of the 50 Foot Woman*. Dr. Cockroach owes a debt to *The Fly*; the Missing Link recalls *Creature from the Black Lagoon*; B.O.B. is a cuddly cousin to *The Blob*; and Insectosaurus combines the giant-bug pictures of the atomic age with the scale and pathos of Japanese kaiju movies. The secret government bunker, alien robot and panic-stricken citizens further evoke the Cold War era, when radiation, outer space and scientific hubris supplied Hollywood with an endless parade of rubber-suited anxieties.

The references are broad enough that children need not recognize them, while adults may enjoy identifying the sources. Even the casting contains a sly genre joke: **Stephen Colbert** voices the President of the United States, who attempts to communicate with an alien robot by playing a keyboard, moving quickly from the famous five-note greeting in *Close Encounters of the Third Kind* to a less dignified selection.

Not all the humor lands. B.O.B.’s absent-minded non sequiturs are reliably amusing, largely because Rogen gives the blob the guileless confidence of someone blissfully unaware of his own limitations. Laurie lends Dr. Cockroach a deliciously exaggerated mad-scientist manner, and Arnett makes the Missing Link’s vanity transparent and funny. But the screenplay often falls back on frantic chatter, topical gags and pop-culture jokes that date more quickly than the vintage films being saluted.

What gives “Monsters vs. Aliens” more substance than its title suggests is Susan’s gradual reassessment of her life. At first she wants only to become small again, escape captivity and resume her wedding plans. Yet her transformation exposes the limits of Derek’s affection: he is comfortable with Susan when she is expected to support his career, less so when she becomes too powerful—literally and figuratively—to remain in his shadow.

The symbolism is hardly subtle, but it is effective. Susan’s size becomes an expression of confidence rather than a condition to be cured. She learns that she can be frightened without being helpless and feminine without being diminished. For a family blockbuster released amid a crowded field of male-centered animated adventures, Ginormica was a welcome protagonist: capable, empathetic and increasingly responsible for her own rescue. Witherspoon’s performance helps prevent the character’s empowerment arc from feeling like a mechanical lesson.

Visually, the film is built for depth and scale. Its original stereoscopic presentation occasionally indulges in objects thrust toward the audience, but the most effective images use 3-D to emphasize Susan’s isolation, the cavernous monster prison and the dizzying dimensions of the Golden Gate Bridge battle. The animation remains colorful and energetic even when the plotting becomes predictable.

Gallaxhar is a comparatively thin villain, and the final act supplies few surprises. Still, the film’s generous spirit carries it through. The monsters, initially presented as threats, emerge as loyal companions; the supposed “normal” world proves capable of selfishness and absurdity; and Susan discovers that becoming monstrous in appearance has allowed her to become more fully herself.

“Monsters vs. Aliens” does not reinvent the animated comedy or the invasion movie. It does, however, combine them with wit, affection and a heroine who stands tall in every sense. At a brisk **94 minutes**, it is an amiable matinee spectacle—noisy, bright and sufficiently warmhearted to outlast many of its punch lines.

**Rated PG** for science-fiction action, some crude humor and mild language. **Running time: 1 hour, 34 minutes.**

counterfactuals.prompt: Pretend you are a cynical CNN film critic reviewing “Monsters vs. Aliens.” Argue that its high concept, celebrity voice cast, and scattered references cannot make up for a limp plot and two-dimensional characters.
counterfactuals.output:
### Review: “Monsters vs. Aliens” Is Big, Loud and Strangely Hollow

“Monsters vs. Aliens” arrives with the sort of title that practically writes the marketing campaign itself. It promises colossal creatures, interplanetary mayhem and enough 3-D debris hurled at the audience to justify the surcharge. What it does not provide is much reason to care.

The premise is efficient, if not especially inspired: Susan Murphy, an ordinary bride-to-be, is struck by a meteorite, grows to nearly 50 feet tall and is promptly imprisoned alongside a government collection of movie-monster knockoffs. When an alien invader threatens Earth, these misfits become humanity’s last defense. Think 1950s science fiction run through a corporate animation blender, with self-esteem lessons added for nutritional value.

The celebrity voice cast is predictably crowded. Reese Witherspoon gives Susan an appealing sincerity; Seth Rogen performs another variation on Seth Rogen as the gelatinous B.O.B.; Hugh Laurie lends dry wit to Dr. Cockroach; Will Arnett growls as the fish-man Missing Link; and Stephen Colbert turns the president into an extended comic sketch. The actors are energetic, but star power is not character development. Most of these figures are one joke with limbs—sometimes several limbs—and the screenplay rarely asks them to become anything more.

Susan receives the closest thing to an arc, moving from anxious fiancée to empowered giant. Yet even that transformation feels assembled from familiar parts. Her shallow boyfriend exists mainly to be discarded, her teammates exist to cheer her on, and the villain exists to announce his plans in a voice that suggests the writers mistook volume for menace.

The film scatters references to old monster movies, science-fiction clichés, political satire and pop culture as if recognition were the same thing as wit. There are nods for parents, slapstick for children and action scenes for everyone checking the time. A few gags land—Colbert’s keyboard encounter is agreeably absurd—but too many simply point at something familiar and wait for applause.

Visually, the movie is polished and perpetually busy. Its battles are colorful, its scale appropriately enormous, and its 3-D effects make a determined effort to poke the audience in the face. But spectacle cannot disguise the limp plot underneath. The story advances with the inevitability of a theme-park ride: introduction, imprisonment, invasion, teamwork, empowerment, explosion.

“Monsters vs. Aliens” has a terrific elevator pitch, an expensive cast and a filing cabinet full of references. What it lacks are memorable personalities, genuine surprise and a story sturdy enough to support all that digital commotion. The monsters may be oversized, but the movie’s imagination is disappointingly small.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a detailed negative review of “Monsters vs. Aliens” that opens with an exaggerated warning to parents, critiques the movie’s physics and animation, mentions “Coraline” and “Space Chimps,” and ends with its PG rating and 94-minute runtime.
counterfactuals.output:
**Parents, lock up your children, barricade the multiplex, and do not let anyone under the age of twelve wander within fifty feet of this aggressively noisy slab of computer-generated mayhem.**

*Monsters vs. Aliens* has a premise that should have been irresistible: a group of misunderstood movie monsters is recruited by the government to defend Earth from an alien invasion. Yet the film turns that promising setup into a frantic chain of chases, crashes, explosions, and obvious punch lines. Rather than developing its oddball heroes or exploring the comic possibilities of classic monster movies, it settles for disposable gags and the increasingly familiar message that being different is secretly wonderful.

The story follows Susan, a bride-to-be who is struck by a meteor and grows to nearly fifty feet tall. Renamed Ginormica and imprisoned in a secret government facility, she meets a gelatinous blob named B.O.B., the aquatic Missing Link, the insect-headed Dr. Cockroach, and the skyscraper-sized Insectosaurus. When the alien Gallaxhar arrives to retrieve the substance that transformed Susan, the monsters are released as humanity’s last line of defense. This is less a narrative than a runway from which the filmmakers launch action sequences.

The movie’s physics are especially ridiculous, even by cartoon standards. Susan changes size without the world around her reacting with any consistency: floors, cars, bridges, and buildings support or collapse beneath her according to the needs of the next gag. Characters fall enormous distances, smash through concrete, and absorb impacts that should flatten them, only to bounce back with barely a pause. Of course, realism is not required in a comedy about giant monsters and alien robots, but good animation usually creates its own coherent physical rules. Here, weight and momentum vanish whenever they become inconvenient. The result is action that feels strangely insubstantial. Nothing has consequences, so nothing produces much suspense.

The animation is polished but unattractive. Surfaces shine, fur and slime are carefully rendered, and the camera swoops through elaborate environments, yet the visual design often looks rubbery and overlit. Susan’s enormous eyes and stiff expressions belong to the generic DreamWorks house style, while Gallaxhar resembles a collection of tubes and tentacles assembled around a celebrity voice performance. The 3-D effects are equally pushy, repeatedly hurling objects toward the audience as if depth alone were a substitute for composition. Technical sophistication is everywhere, but personality is scarce.

That deficiency becomes clearer beside *Coraline*, another animated release from the same period. *Coraline* uses texture, color, scale, and movement to build a distinctive world with genuine atmosphere and danger. *Monsters vs. Aliens* uses its visual resources mainly to make things loom, whiz, and explode. It is certainly slicker than the dreary *Space Chimps*, but that is a painfully low standard; both films confuse frantic motion and noisy wisecracks with imaginative storytelling.

The voice cast works hard. Reese Witherspoon gives Susan warmth, Seth Rogen makes B.O.B. cheerfully dim, Hugh Laurie lends Dr. Cockroach some comic precision, and Stephen Colbert amusingly exaggerates the president’s vanity and incompetence. But the characters rarely rise above a single defining trait. B.O.B. is stupid, Missing Link is macho, Dr. Cockroach is eccentric, and Gallaxhar is megalomaniacal. Their banter produces occasional laughs, but the script keeps announcing personalities instead of deepening them.

Even Susan’s potentially meaningful journey is simplified into a blunt lesson about self-esteem. Her transformation allows her to discover that her fiancé is shallow and that her monstrous new friends are loyal, but these developments are so predictable that the emotional climax arrives prepackaged. The movie wants applause for telling Susan she does not need an inadequate man to define her, yet it gives her little inner life beyond that realization.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is not incompetent, and very young viewers may enjoy its bright colors, broad slapstick, and colossal destruction. But it is a factory-built entertainment: loud, efficient, technically accomplished, and instantly forgettable. It offers monsters without menace, aliens without mystery, and spectacle without weight.

**Rated PG; 94 minutes.**
